The Address-Mr. Smith (Calgary West)
late because, if rumour and certain statements we have read, are accurate, he has not acted soon enough.
Turning to the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters), I find that he did not make that mistake. It was clear that he complemented everyone he thought might ever wear a red carnation. No, he left out no one, at all. However, I pay him a special compliment and it is this: I realize that in the House of Commons there are some great linguists, some dialectical giants; but his French was the only French I have understood since I came here.
But I am not going to stop there in my felicitations, because I noted that when, following the speech of my leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) addressed the house, he complimented two of our number who richly deserve the very fine distinction which has been granted them.
I say nothing about .the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) for two reasons: First, he is in my profession, and second, he might catch me out. But I am going to say something about the right hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) of which, I am quite sure, none of you Eastern people are aware. This might constitute an additional reason, why His Majesty saw fit so to honour him. Out in Western Canada the minister is known as a second Michael Angelo, the greatest painter of his time. By that I mean simply this, that one needs only to drive through Alberta these days in order to see that every farm building is beautifully painted with money the farmers took away from the Minister of Finance because they could charge it up against their tax. So that at least by volume, in any event, he is the greatest modern painter.
Then the Prime Minister, perhaps thinking that some other member of his flock had been slightly overlooked, took care to compliment the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe), and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). And in the blushing contest which followed the thing I observed most closely was that the Minister of Labour won, in a walk. There can be no doubt about it.
Speaking seriously for myself-and I believe I might speak in this respect for all new members in the house-I wish to compliment and thank all the senior members in all parties for the great kindnesses they have shown and the help they have given to those of us who for the first time came here last September.
I intend to mention only one feature of the speech from the throne, that having to do with veterans' housing. I hope to be helpful, 
and I am quite sure this may mean something to those in authority. We have been told all over Canada that we cannot get housing for veterans. There is in my home city of Calgary a radio station called CFAC which has a good idea. Those of us who come from there or who live near there know it is impossible to get accommodation, but this station has devoted fifteen minutes of its time during afternoons to interviewing veterans and their wives and families, if there are families, who are seeking accommodation. The offer made by the station was enthusiastically accepted by Mr. White, secretary of the rehabilitation council there. The result was that when the first programme period was completed the telephone started ringing and six offers of accommodation came in. That particular couple were placed as well as two other families. This continued from January 14 until February 15, during which time twenty-five veterans were interviewed, 101 replies were were received and ninety homeless veterans with their families were placed.
I think that record speaks for itself. It takes care of one of our major difficulties in finding housing accommodation for these people. Many people would be glad to open their homes or rent flats now available in their homes if they were sure of the type of people who would occupy them. I know ninety-nine per cent of our veterans are splendid people, but there is the odd bad apple in every barrel, particularly in Ontario apples, although this does not happen in British Columbia. The simple fact is that that excellent response was obtained in thirty days. Why? Because the people who had accommodation listened to the personal interviews that were carried on by the radio man named Jack Stewart, and they were able to get some idea of the type of people who were seeking accommodation. I am just giving that to the proper minister because it seems to me that if that practice were followed, especially in our larger cities, it might take care of a great deal of our veteran housing problem.
I turn now to a subject on which I intend to speak, not at length but only for a few minutes. I am referring to this espionage matter. I begin by giving you, sir, and the house my undertaking that my language will be temperate. I do not intend to accuse anyone of a violation of good faith or anything of that sort, nor will I say anything which might be interpreted, when coming from a humble private member, as having anything to do with international relations. But I do intend to criticize the course which has been adopted, and I trust that it will be

The Address-Mr. Smith (Calgary West)
based on at least some reason. The farthest that I intend to go is to say that I think a serious mistake may have been made.
Having said that, I wish to dispose at once of the criticism which may be made because I criticize the government's action. I say at once that I have no sympathy with people who break the Official Secrets Act. One small change in the circumstances and they would be traitors, they would be guilty of treason and liable to be hanged. If that circumstance were changed, in other words if this were an enemy country, they would richly deserve that most severe punishment of our law. With that I leave it.
But I do mention this: When I read this first in the paper and as I listened last evening to the explanation of the right hon. Prime Minister, I took a look at a book which I had read years ago. This was a book published in 1935,-written by Sinclair Lewis and called "It Can't Happen Here." You cannot get it because I have the library copy at the moment, but I recommend that book to hon. members as preferred reading because it illustrates how a subversive movement requires much less than a majority occasionally to operate a country.
What has happened? In this Dominion of Canada we have watched our nation grow. I do not think there are any here who remember when we were a colony, nor do I think there are any wrho remember when we became a dominion. My mathematics are not very good, but it seems to me that 1867 is quite a considerable time ago. Then we came along to the Statute of Westminster which, after all, did nothing more than declare an existing state of affairs. In other words, our growth has been healthy; it has been constitutional. Any change in status or growth in status at all times has been in conformity with the British .way and with the unanimous consent of the British government, of the British House of Commons and the House of Lords.
We find ourselves grown up, and to prove that we are really out of our swaddling clothes and short pants, that we are now mature as a nation, we have this spy scare. We used to read about this sort of thing in books that I remember that had to do with the mythical kingdom of Graustark. I can remember that those books were beautifully illustrated. There was always a princess who was going to be abused, but the right man came along at the right time and the kingdom of Graustark still went merrily on. It is too bad that one cannot deal with the matter which now confronts
us with a light touch but, as the Prime Minister so well said last evening, that is something which just cannot be done.
What has happened historically is this. On September 5 last, or early in September some time, the Prime Minister became apprised of some information in the hands of a man who was an employee of some sort in the Russian embassy here. The only point I make about that is this:	That information has been in
the hands of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for a period of over five months. Lest anyone think I have any doubts to the contrary, it was in the hands of one of the ablest police organization^ that this world, let alone this country, has ever known. They are an organization with plenty of money and plenty of brains. I have seen their laboratory in Regina and I know they have the finest instruments than one can imagine. I ran squarely up against it not long ago when a man made some photographs of paint that had come from here and there and elsewhere which startled me, and I thought I knew something about criminal investigation. I mention that in passing merely to show that this matter was in splendid hands, in able hands, in the hands of people who times without number had coped with serious crime in this country.
The first document which I mention is the first order in council which was issued I think early in October. The reason I mention that now, and I am going to come back to it, is that by that order in council government policy was set. Nothing that happened after altered the position which was then taken.
I now leave a direct discussion of what took place on this occasion and turn to a bit of history which I think all of us may very well remember. That has been the development in British countries of the position of an accused person before the law. Under magna charta it was provided that a man should have a fair trial and a speedy trial, and in all the developments in our law from that day to this the trend has been in the direction of throwing safeguards around accused persons whose liberty might be at stake. I know it is very easy to snipe at lawyers and say that we are archaic and bound by this and that and never learn anything new, but the common law has been and is constantly growing and has fairly well kept pace with new developments in this or in any other country. I refer to this one fact. Up to within the last eighteen months in any event we always said that if an accused person's statement were to be used against him-a statement made to a person in authority as a police officer

the onus was on
84	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Smith (Calgary'West)
the crown to show that that statement was voluntary, and among other considerations by the court in coming to that conclusion was whether or not warning had been given to the accused as to what his position was. In short, he was told that he was not obliged to say anything. He had nothing to hope in the way of favour and nothing to fear, and what he said might be used against him. That is as close to the short warning used by the mounted police as I can remember. But in the case of Rex v. Gach the Supreme Court of Canada in a judgment written by or concurred in by Mr. Justice Taschereau, now sitting on this commission, the court held that it was a rule of -law-not just one of the things to be considered but a rule of law

that no statement made by an accused person to a person in authority could be used against him without that warning having been given.
I mention that to show the trend there has been in our administration. I think Canada is the only country that has gone thus far in looking after the constitutional right and the interest of the person who is accused of a crime.
I now go a step farther and say this. Everything we have by way of administration is based' on the innocence of the individual until the crown proves him guilty. That has been the corner-stone of everything we have done. You may have a little different superstructure here or a little change there, but that basic fact has never changed from the time we administered criminal law in any British country since magna charta.
Let us compare that with what obtains in some other countries. I do not make this comparison in a disparaging way or to be critical of other countries, because other countries certainly have the full right of setting up their own method of handling the administration of criminal justice. Let us go to France and see what happens. We will say that a person is suspected, an information is laid, and he is arrested. The first thing, that happens to him there is that he is taken before what is known as an- examining magistrate, and that examination is in camera, and it is indeed a real examination. We saw repercussions of it in the recent trial of Mr. Laval, and I am quite sure that it was not edifying to those of us who are accustomed to our own system.
Go to the United States of America. Today in many states of that union there is not even a preliminary hearing. In fact, in famous oases reported in their press I have- seen it said that the crown had a star secret witness up its sleeve, and so on.

Our position has been so different. Here a man is entitled to a preliminary hearing. He is entitled without cost in all the provinces of Canada, if he has no money, to get a copy of everything that was said. In the event that the crown discovers witnesses between the preliminary hearing and the trial the accused is entitled to a full statement from the crown counsel of everything he may say. That has been the British way of proceeding, and with what result? If we take the number of persons charged with crime in this country or in Great Britain and compare it with the numbers in the other countries I have mentioned, and take the number of convictions under our generous treatment here-you may not logically justify some of it, I know-our convictions compare five to one as against those of one other country I have mentioned and tw'enty to one as against those of one great state in that union. I suggest that that must give us an idea of just how fine this method is which we have had in administering our criminal law.
Now I intend to discuss what took place in this case, and with respect, Mr. Speaker, may I ask you now to declare it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess

Doctor May. He was arrested and charged in Bow Street the following morning. What does a man or woman want when he or she is arrested? Let us assume that they have not had my experience and have never been in gaol before. They go in there and are locked up by themselves. What do they want? The man first wants to see his wife, and then his
86	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Smith (Calgary West)
lawyer. The woman wants to see her husband, and then he tells her that she needs a lawyer just because she is there. I am sure that the Postmaster General will agree with me. that counsel is sought in ninety-nine cases out of every one hundred when they have never been in the toils of the law before. That is a natural human reaction. I am going to assume that these people reacted humanly and naturally; that they were the same as everybody else and sought assistance. They did not get it.
Then a royal commission was appointed. I am not going to say anything at all against this royal commission. I am fortunate in having the acquaintanceship of the two judges; I am fortunate in having the friendship of Mr. E. K. Williams of Winnipeg. Both of these judges and Mr. Williams are highly respected in Canada in matters of civil law, but I do not think anyone of the three ever had very much to do with criminal matters.
What about Mr. Fauteux?

That does not apply to Mr. Fauteux. I think I heard an hon. member mention his name. He is one of the ablest prosecutors in Canada; but I leave the word "prosecutor" to rest just where the Postmaster General called it to my attention. There is not a word of criticism in my mind about the motives or about the honesty of purpose of these men; yet I ask this simple question: why was it that two judges of the Supreme Court of Canada were chosen when the appeals may ultimately come before that court? Why not two judges away from the industrial section, because apparently all these questions mentioned in the report of the commissioners apply to the industrial section of Canada? Why not someone from out there? I am not saying for a moment that either Mr. Justice Taschereau or Mr. Justice Kellock would sit on this appeal. They certainly would not; they respect their profession and their position too much to do that, but why were judges taken from a court to which in the ultimate end of proceedings this matter might come for final adjudication?
Let no one think I am saying that when the Minister of Justice chose these fine gentlemen to carry on this work he had anything in his mind of a nature which was not of the best. The most that I have said or ever will say about this matter is that in my opinion a terrible mistake has been made.
We were told by the Prime Minister that these people were offered counsel. I have no doubt that they were. The commissioners say in their report that they did it in conformity

with sections 12 and 13 of the act respecting inquiries. I am going to read those sections because they are very short:
12.	The commissioners may allow any person whose conduct is being investigated under this Act, 'and sballl allow any person-
The first is "may", the second is "shall".
-against whom 'any charge is mode in the course of such investigation, to be represented by counsel.
13.	No report shall be made against any person until reasonable notice shall have been- given to him of the charge of misconduct alleged *against him 'and he shall have been' tallowed full opportunity to be heard in person or by counsel1.
Something that I think we need to be told is this. I gathered!-and if I am wrong I hope I shall be immediately corrected-that once these men had given, evidence before this commission they were offered counsel. I gathered that from the Prime Minister's remarks and from reading reports of this commisison. If that be so, let us hark back to the main principle upon which justice has been administered. Here you have people already in gaol, in solitary confinement with a man at the door. We heard something about failure to attempt suicide and that sort of thing. The man at the door is the only person they ever saw. They have never been in gaol before. They are brought before this commission. There you have two supreme court judges whose names are well known, and who are no doubt known to them, eminent andi able counsel, clerks, secretaries, stenographers and all that sort of thing which go with royal commissions, and they were largely meant for us lawyers, generally speaking. But you have all this. These people come in singly, and what happens? They are examined under oath. If the newspaper report of the other day was correct they are sworn to secrecy as to what happened there. True, it is only a report in one of the Ottawa papers, and I do not know whether or not it is true, but that is what was said. What in the world is the good of offering people counsel after they have been in solitary confinement, after they have been examined by this commission?
You and I, Mr. Speaker, and all other hon. members know there is nothing so aimed to break down will power and voluntary action as solitary confinement and being rushed in before a tribunal of that kind. Under these circumstances no one suggests that these would be voluntary statements. To my mind, and I think the Postmaster General will agree with me, it is absolute nonsense. People need counsel before they are aiming for trouble, and before people are trying to cause them

The Address-Mr. Smith (Calgary West)
trouble. Those are the people who need the protection of people who by their training are expert in giving them advice in that way.

I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but he has already spoken for forty minutes.

speechtext: I hope Your Honour will allow the hon. member to proceed; I am sure it is the wash of the house.

I am sorry, sir, to have broken a rule and my promise that I would not speak for more than fifteen minutes, but time seems to get away from me. We did not commence our session until about five minutes after eight, sir, I would point out with the greatest of respect.
All I have to go on are the newspaper reports. I assure you, sir, and everyone in this House of Commons that I have not communicated with any of these accused nor have I communicated in any way, directly or indirectly, with counsel for any of the accused. So that I am speaking entirely from the record and from what I have read in the Ottawa newspapers only. I have not enough money to subscribe to the Globe and Mail, which I am told supports our side.
Just what has happened? We read in the newspapers that when Mrs. Woikin, the lady who came from Blaine Lake in Saskatchewan, appeared before the magistrate she was quite distracted and greatly disturbed, and endeavoured to plead guilty. I do not know Magistrate Strike but he must be an awfully good chap, because he refused to accept that plea. That was the physical and mental condition of this woman after having gone through experiences which I can perhaps better imagine than speak about. I am not going to use my imagination, but I have some idea of the things that run through the minds of people who are incarcerated in lonely silence.
We are told by the Prime Minister that they were waiting for Doctor May-I gather that it would be Doctor May-who was going to England1 in October to make a certain contact. Well, the mounted police are practical people; I have never known them to be naive. In September Gouzenko moves out with an armful of files and documents. This other man leaves Canada in October, and we waited to see if he would make a contact. Well, nobody is quite that dumb.

Thank you. My point is that a month passed by. Let us consider the Russian embassy, which was engineering this spy ring. Gouzenko is gone; all their documents are gone. Who would think that Doctor May would make his contact in London under such circumstances? No one is quite that dumb. That is a simple statement of the situation.
I have said a word already about the plea of the hon. member for Cartier and the plea of Doctor May. Now I continue. How regular this procedure is! Will not our minds go back to the first great war when hon. members will remember Mr. Von Papen ran the German embassy in the United States? This whole thing seems to fall into line with that sort of thing. I am almost through, sir, and will not trespass much longer on your generosity.
What does this all mean? In short, what is my complaint? Many years ago one of the greatest judges in English law said something that has never been disputed in any courthouse in the Dominion of Canada; that in the administration of justice it is better that ten guilty men go free than that one innocent man be convicted. Do not for a moment think I do not agree that we need a royal commission. I believe we need something to purge the government offices of this country of people like those who have been turned up in this particular business. I think it is also time that in employing civil servants scholastic attainments should not be given the greatest consideration in appointing people to positions of responsibility. I go farther in my effort to be fair and say that of course this sort of thing is entirely new in this country. But I am asking you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members of this house to imagine the normal procedure under the law. In September we had the information, and an excellent police force which worked over it for five months. Now what happens? It is not of very great importance if two or three persons should escape imprisonment. Of course we have the statement by the Prime Minister at page 51 of Hansard that the idea of the continuation was to see that no one should escape the net. That is not nearly so important as that we should maintain what has really made us what we are, in other words the rule of law in everything we do. What is law? Law is nothing more than the codification of honesty in business and good morals in social conduct;

The Address-Mr. St. Laurent
and I do not see why we have not been able to proceed along that line in the good old way. Surely the. deputy ministers of the various departments in which these things have gone wrong are in a position to make a purge of their own departments. If we ever needed a house-cleaning we need it now. Surely it is not a matter of great importance that two or three individuals might escape punishment.
May I close by saying just this. It is true that we have had this commission. It is true that persons have been suspected of crime because, as the Prime Minister indicated, the documents pointed to them. It is true that they have been brought before the commission without warning, without protection, without an opportunity to see their families or to get legal advice. In six months, Mr. Speaker, this spy scare will be forgotten. Unfortunately our people are a bit too apathetic about matters of this kind. But I say to you, sir, that during your lifetime and mine the people of this country will always regret and will never live down the fact that we threw aside and abrogated the rights and liberties of our citizens. Indeed, sir, Canada now has seen black days.
Right Hon. L. S. St. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, I expected that we would hear some pretty strong criticism of what it was found necessary to do under the extraordinary conditions this government has had to face in connection with what I think I may describe, without violating any rule as to matters being sub judice, as a conspiracy for the establishment of a dangerous fifth column in this country. I would have been disappointed had that criticism not been made; because it is good, when extraordinary measures are taken, that they should be looked at very closely, and that those who venture to take them should feel that they have to respond to the tribunal of public opinion for those actions of which they have been the authors.
But I did not expect that it would take the line that has been indicated in the last few remarks of the hon. member who has just taken' his seat. For almost five years now I have occupied the office to which the leader of my party did me the honour to call me. It was my good fortune during the whole period of the war not to have been called upon to exercise any of the powers that had been conferred upon the incumbent of that office by the defence of Canada regulations.
Those regulations were quite drastic. Under them drastic action had been taken. But whether it be because drastic action had been taken or not, this country went through six years of war without any sabotage, and

without any incident that retarded the effect of the will of the large majority of the people to put forth a gallant and valiant effort in the struggle, for the maintenance of our institutions.
After I came into office it did happen that on two occasions internment orders had to be made. I suppose it was childish on my part, but I did take some satisfaction from the fact that, through no pre-arrangement, it so happened that I was not in Ottawa at the time those orders had to be made. And it was with great satisfaction that, when the war came to a close, I felt that the only orders I had been called upon to sign under those regulations were orders putting an end to the detentions that had been brought about under them.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat has said that he was speaking from the record; and it is quite natural that, in doing so, some discrepancies may creep into the facts as one states them. It is not the fact that the events narrated last night by the Prime Minister came to the knowledge of the Minister of Justice on that first day, when this Mr. Gouzenko tried to impart the information.
On the morning of September 6 he came to my secretary and asked for an interview. Being unknown to my secretary, as is the practice he was asked to state what his business was. When afterwards I was informed as to what his business was, I immediately said I could not receive an official from a friendly embassy bearing tales of the kind he had described to my secretary. And it was only after the police of the city of Ottawa requested the assistance of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that, in the ordinary course of the exercise of their duties, which includes the giving of assistance to local authorities when called upon, they were put in possession of some of these facts.
We did hear that among those facts was the narration of an arrangement made for a contact to take place in London on a certain date, at a certain hour, at a certain street comer, -where parties were to be recognized, with all the frills of an Oppenheim detective story-a newspaper under the left arm, or carried in one's pocket in a certain fashion, and by the exchange of greetings in terms which had been determined upon.
It did not seem to me probable, after this Mr. Gouzenko had disappeared, that this meeting would take place. Nevertheless, one of the gentlemen concerned did leave Canada on the date that the pre-arrangement indicated would be the date of his departure. I did not ttink much would come of it; but

The Address-Mr. St. Laurent
on October 6 we were requested to be ready to take action here in Canada if an arrest were made in London on the following evening. It is under those conditions that the order in council printed in this white paper was made.
The meeting did not take place; and I felt a substantial relief from the fact that the provisions made in this order did not have to be carried into effect. I had other matters to attend to, I never saw that order again until after the order in council appointing the royal commission was made, and counsel for the commission came to me asking me to sign orders for the detention and interrogation of certain persons. We then had a quite lengthy discussion over it, and I told them that if the order were one that was going to be made, then it would not be in that form; that I did not think in peace time it was proper that any member of the executive should have the kind of powers the order expressed; that I thought no one should be detained, even for interrogation, without there being some form of intervention of the judicial authority; that we would act only as if that were the provision, and that there would have to be a recommendation from some organ of the judicial authority to make me feel that I should exercise those powers.
It went so far that I was finally asked if I was going to take the responsibility of refusing to exercise them. I felt that that responsibility would be a responsibility for the safety of the state, whilst the other would be merely a responsibility that might involve some political discredit, and that between the two I would choose to assume whatever political criticism might be directed against me for following the advice I got from counsel for the commission, acting on instructions from the commission.
I shall now refer to the statute from which my hon. friend read. I do not think there is anyone in this house who will disagree with anything the hon. member has said with respect to the prosecution of individuals. But does not the hon. gentleman realize that there is more than the prosecution of individuals involved in this investigation? Does not the hon. member realize that the Inquiries Act was put into the statutes precisely to take care of situations which concerned the safety or good administration of the state, whilst all provisions which deal with the prosecution or otherwise of individuals who have committed offences are in the criminal code? What was required here was not some form of prosecution of an individual; what was required when
it was determined by this magnificent body to which the hon. member has paid tribute, the officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, that this was something serious was a commission to determine the extent to which it had vitiated the administrative life of this free country. It is for that reason that the commission was appointed to inquire into the matter.
The hon. member has stated before the house that a serious mistake was made in the selection of the commissioners, in choosing two justices of the Supreme Court of Canada instead of taking some other justices from some other courts in Canada. Well, I am willing to submit our judgment about the selection of those commissioners to the country as against the judgment of the hon. member for Calgary West.
You can submit it in Calgary West at any time you want to.

And in many other spots too.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It so happens that this is the spot it has to be submitted to at this time. We in this house represent no spot; we represent the whole of Canada. The Inquiries Act, which is chapter 99 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, was placed on the statute books by the parliament of Canada for the purposes which are described in the statute. It provides:
The governor in council may, whenever he deems it expedient, cause inquiry to fee made into land concerning any matter connected with the good government of Canada or the conduct of laoy paoit of the public business thereof.
That is not the criminal code. That is a statute passed to enable the governor in council to have an investigation made under conditions which -will satisfy him, the parliament and the public of Canada that it is being proceeded with in a fair, judicial, careful and prudent manner. For the purpose of making that investigation the government of Canada was happy to follow the advice of the gentleman referred to by the hon. member, whom both he and I know well and than whom no one stands higher in his profession in this country. That gentleman at the present time is the president of the Canadian Bar Association. His first suggestion was that the commissioners be three members of the Supreme Court of Canada, and he afterwards modified that to the extent of recommending that two commissioners might be sufficient for the purposes of this commission. It was his opinion, an opinion which commended itself to His

The Address-Mr. St. Laurent
Excellency's advisers, an opinion which I think will commend itself to this house, that it was proper to ask these two gentlemen who are now the commissioners to undertake that service, that onerous and disagreeable service to the public of Canada, which this royal commission has to perform.
They made an examination of the papers which had been handed over to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police by this man Gouzenko under the conditions which were described last evening by the right hon. the Prime Minister and which I will not repeat. They came to the conclusion that there was no doubt about the authenticity of those documents. Not many of them have yet been published and I cannot speak of those that have not been published. This investigation is proceeding in camera, but they came to the conclusion that taking these documents as authentic it was necessary for the purposes of a full and complete investigation that certain persons be detained for interrogation and they recommended that that be done.
I did not think at the time it was going to take as long as it is taking. It has really been a disappointment that it was necesasry to hold these persons so long before they could be interrogated and the commissioners make their final report. That is unfortunate, not as much for the persons who are detained, although they have my full sympathy, as for the public opinion of this country. It has made it appear that the important question before the country at the present time was not whether the security of the state was being undermined by the infiltration of this fifth column into many of the public offices but whether there had been anything done which might be prejudicial to an accused person when he came before the court of justice. We are all as attached as the hon. member for Calgary West to the proper administration of justice, whether it be criminal or civil, as it has been practised under the British system which has become our own, but there has been nothing shown anywhere which constitutes any violation of any right which any individual may have when he comes to answer for any charge brought against him.
One person not reported against by the commission, who could not be reported against because he had not been heard by the commission and because he could not be called upon to appear before the commission, was mentioned in the evidence that was put before the crown prosecutor for the purpose of making charges against some one who had been heard and who had been examined. Counsel retained came to the conclusion that it would not be proper to prosecute one person for con-
spiracy with the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Rose) without at the same time bringing charges against him. Those charges were laid, an arrest was made and the next morning he appeared before the court in Montreal and within a very few hours was released on bail.
Doctor A. N. May was arrested in London, certainly as much as three weeks ago, and the Ottawa Journal's five o'clock edition today reports:
Bail refused for Dr. A. N. Hay in London Court-British scientist held for trial in s>py case.
London, March 19.-Dr. Allan Nunn May, 34-year-old British physicist who worked in Canada on nuclear research in the war-time pursuit of atomic energy, to-day was held for trial in Old Bailey Orimdniail Court, April 13, on charges of violating the Official Secrets Act hy giving atomic information to an undisclosed person.
Dr. M.ay was refused bail by Magistrate McKenna of Bow Street Court, who said the defendant's release might be "against public policy."
Doctor May, like everybody else, is deemed to be innocent until found guilty, but Doctor May was refused, pending further investigation of the charges against him, to be allowed his temporary freedom on bail because it might be against public policy.
Here the royal commissioners held that it would be against public policy and would be apt to defeat the basic purposes for which this basic investigation had been instituted if the persons they wished to interrogate were not detained pending their interrogation. That has taken more time than we hoped it might take, but there was only one of two courses to follow. One would have been to treat this as of not sufficient importance to warrant any other action than perhaps a discreet dismissal of those who might be suspected of having engaged in. the spying proceedings. The other was to take steps to make sure that we would ascertain, as far as it is possible to do so, to what extent this virus had penetrated into branches of the public service and, as is suggested to me, throughout the country at large. We knew that there would be serious political embarrassment for us in taking the latter course. One of the most embarrassing features about public life that I have been up against in the short time that I have been in it is the necessity of making decisions based upon facts you know but cannot fully disclose to the public. This is not the first time that I have been up against that difficulty. Some hon. members were here in 1944 when I had to take a stand based upon the facts which I knew and which in my opinion fully justified the stand I took, but at that time those facts could not be made known. Last May it was possible to go to places where my conduct

The Address-Mr. St. Laurent
had been severely criticized and tell them then the facts which I knew at the time I made the decision and to say to them: Is there any one of you here who, had you been in my place and had known those facts, would not have done as I did? And I got a satisfactory answer.
This is another occasion where we are not free at the present time to disclose more than has been disclosed by public statements or by this white paper. We had to make a decision, well knowing that in the meantime it would involve the probability of criticism, the probability of serious criticism. My colleagues know to what extent I pointed out what criticism we would be up against when we had to defend this line of conduct, but I am confident that the public of Canada when this thing is over will, as did the public of other parts of Canada last May, feel that we took the right course, the courageous course, the only course under which it was possible to satisfy the responsibility we had for the safety of government-I do not mean the government of a party but the safety of our form of government in this country.
With respect to individuals, whenever the moment arises for them to have to answer to the charges against them, even before an adverse report is made about them by the commission, they are brought before the commissioners as required by these sections read by the hon. member are told what the facts are which indicate that they should be critically reported upon by the commissioners and are asked if they wish to have counsel. They are told that they are free to adduce further evidence if they see fit to do so, and after that they are not found guilty because the royal commission has no power to find anyone guilty or to impose any sentence upon anyone. The royal commission makes a report, and on that report the government has to take the responsibility, as the Prime Minister said in his statement of February 15 it would take, of determining whether or not such person will be prosecuted.

Will the
minister permit a simple question? Was it after they had been examined under oath that they were given that opportunity?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is after they are examined under oath that they are given that opportunity. They are examined under oath, not to determine whether they have done anything personally, but to inform the commission what they know about the extent of this conspiracy as it affects the body politic.

Including themselves.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Including themselves and including the rest of the 11,500,000 or 12,000,000 Canadians.

Agreed, but about 11,999,990 of the others are out of gaol, are they not?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: This investigation had to be made or had to be omitted. I would not have taken the responsibility of passing over the information that was characterized by the experienced members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as -being probably authentic.
Some suggestion has been made that we first heard of this in September and that it was not until February that a royal commission was set up. In due time full explanations will be available to the Canadian public for that delay, and when those explanations are available I think the Canadian public will find them satisfactory.
The Prime Minister indicated last night that we did not feel that this country should be made the base for spying out information affecting our neighbours to the south or affecting the United Kingdom, and that it was proper to communicate to them beforehand such information as was available. The information on which Doctor A. N. May was charged was information obtained at the same time in the same way, and those proceedings, hon. members will recall, coincided with the institution of proceedings here. It was felt, and I think properly so, that our action should be synchronized with all such action as might be taken elsewhere arising out of the same set of facts.
The hon. member says that a great judge has stated that it would be better that ten guilty persons should escape condemnation than that one innocent person be found guilty of an offence which he did not commit. That is all very well, and that is no doubt the rule which will be followed and strictly applied in the courts of justice before which this case will have to appear. But in this royal commission the purpose was not to pronounce upon the innocence or guilt of any of ten or thirteen or more persons but to find out to what extent the security of this state had been endangered by a conspiracy to set up this fifth column in our country. I submit, and I take full responsibility for the view, that when gentlemen such as the two members of the royal commission, such as the eminent counsel who have been associated with them, report that the only effective way to make the investigation which the circum-

The Address-Mr. St. Laurent
stances require is to detain and interrogate persons who may have knowledge about it, it wat proper to accept that advice and to proceed with that investigation.
Had it not been at this time it could not have been done in that way. It was done in that way only because it so happened that an order in council which had been made on October 6, 1945, was still in force. If there had been no legal way of doing it I would have felt no responsibility. But when there was a legal way, when there was a way by which it could legally be done, I could not take the responsibility of refusing to comply with the advice which was given to me. I will not say I was happy that there was a legal way of doing it. It would have been much more comfortable for me to be able to say, "This cannot legally be done".
Reference has been made to the excluding of habeas corpus. That is not technically correct. There has been no setting aside of the statute of Charles providing for habeas corpus. All that the habeas corpus statute provides for is that anyone who is detained may require that he be brought before a judge so that the judge will determine whether or not there is a legal case for his detention. Any one of these persons could have applied for and obtained a writ of habeas corpus, but it would have done him no good, because as soon as the judge would have been shown the order in council under which such person was detained, and the order in council which authorized it, he would have said, "You are legally detained". And that would have required the quashing of the wrrit. So that no writ of habeas corpus would have had any practical effect under these proceedings, any more than the writ of habeas corpus which was issued during the last war and which was the occasion for the leading case that decides the effect of the War Measures Act.
The writ was issued and it went through to the Supreme Court of Canada, and the decision was that things done under the War Measures Act had the effect of a statute to provide a legal cause for the detention of the man. The same would have happened here. The writ of habeas corpus is not set aside. There is provision for the detention of an individual, something which is not according to the ordinary rules of law, and if it is regularly provided by parliament, or under the authority of parliament, it requires the writ to be quashed just as effectively as if it were a conviction in an ordinary court.

Will the minister permit a. question? Will he tell us how a person held incommunicado could bring a writ of habeas corpus?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: My hon. friend is himself a lawyer and he does not need my advice-	.

A lawyer, not a magician.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: -as to how that could be done. It is no business of the custodian of a person who is held to provide opportunities for the issuing of these writs. There may be facts which create difficulties in the way of having a writ. One could imagine, for instance, someone being arrested and detained . in the wilderness of the north.

Not in Canada.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It would not be easy for him to have a writ issued, but that would not mean that he did not have his legal right to the writ. These are circumstances which result from the facts, but they create no legal obstacle.	*
There is just one other point to which I wish to refer. It is personal. I do not like to have to refer to it but I think I should. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) called attention to a statement I made in the crossfire of discussion when the emergency powers bill was being debated in committee on December 6 last. There had been some discussion there over a secret order in council providing for the examination of seamen. It was an order which it was alleged had not been published but had been tabled in this house about a month before. I said that was not a secret order and that there were no secret orders. The leader of the opposition was kind enough to say he was quite convinced I had not meant to mislead the house, and I hoped no one in the house would believe that on any occasion I would wish to mislead the house. I had no thought at that time of this order, which had not been used, which had been prepared for use in the event that this rendezvous which the hon. member for Calgary West says no one would have been dumb enough to keep after Gouzenko had abstracted certain papers from the Russian embassy had not taken place.
As I said before, I felt a great relief that no orders were required to be made under this, and it had entirely slipped my memory. Had I thought of it at any time since and looked at it, I would have been inclined, before December 31, before the date when the War Measures Act ceased to be operative, to have had it modified, to require the proceedings which in fact I did ask to have accom-

The Address-Mr. St. Laurent
plished before I signed any orders, because once again I do not think a member of the executive branch of government should in peace time have powers of that nature that he can exercise of his own volition. It is only very rarely that any extraordinary proceedings can be taken, because the whole of the normal legislation has to be statutory, and there is nothing in the Inquiries Act which authorizes the detention of persons for interrogation. They are compelled to appear. They are not allowed counsel unless the commissioners feel that they should have them. This denial of counsel of which so much has been made is something which has been provided by this parliament before the hon. member for Calgary West or the member for Quebec East came into this parliament. This parliament decided that in cases of royal inquiries the right to counsel would exist from a given moment. Parliament [DOT]determined that up to that moment it would be discretionary for the commissioners as to whether those called before them would have counsel or not.

They may.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The commissioners may do it, but they are not required to do it, and they may refuse to do it.

They did,
apparently.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: And they did; but in doing that they were carrying out a provision passed by this parliament which has stood on the statute book for a great many years.

It was never intended to track down spies.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Un.til quite recently in this country it was never thought that any government would have to track down spies in its own service, and I hope that from this time onward the result of this commission will be such that that unpleasant duty will never fall upon any other government. But if it does and should it at any time again become necessary I hope there will be in office a government that will not shirk the responsibility of doing its duty.

I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) on his feet. Would he permit me to ask the Minister of Justice a question? I suggested last evening that two persons who had been held had been treated in a particular manner. To-night the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) referred to it. Would the minister tell us what he knows about it? I think it is something that should be cleared up^

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I fully agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Had it been possible for me to get to the Department of Justice to-day I would have been in a position to give the answer. Unfortunately I was not able to get to the department today. There was a meeting of the treasury board at half-past nine o'clock, and from that moment until this it has not been possible for me to get to the responsible officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to find out exactly what are the facts in that regard. I know that I discussed with the commissioner at the outset the treatment to be accorded to these persons, and we both agreed that they should be subjected to as little inconvenience as possible, and that we should endeavour in' our representations to the commission and to the counsel to make .the duration of that inconvenience as short as possible. I shall make inquiry, but I shall not promise to give the answer to-morrow, because I think it is serious enough for the commissioner to make a full inquiry and have before him all those who were in charge of the persons who were being detained for interrogation.

May I be permitted to ask a question? When the minister was speaking he corrected the hon. member for Calgary West with respect to one factual matter. The hon. member for Calgary West thought that the matter had been brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice in September last. The minister said that was an error, but he did not tell us when it was brought to his attention.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: In a general way it was reported to me on the following day.

Oh, oh.
Mr. _ST. LAURENT: Hon. members need not laugh. I am trying to give the leader of the opposition the full facts as I am sure he would like to have them. If it is not suitable to other hon, members that I give them to him here I shall be glad to give them to him privately. The day after Gouzenko's visit to my secretary I was informed that the Ottawa police had requested the assistance of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police about this man, and I told them then they were free to see him and to get the story from him. Then as it developed in the course of a few following days I was apprised from time to time of what information was being obtained.

When was the first day?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It was .the day of the opening of the house, September 6, and on September 7 I was told that this same man
The Address-Speaker's Ruling

who had tried to see them the day previous, and with respect to whom I had told them that they must not see him, had been brought to them through the instrumentality of the Ottawa police.

Was that contrary to what the hon. member for Calgary West said?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I think so. I gathered from the hon. member that he was under the impression that I had received this Mr. Gouzenko and had heard his story when he came from the Russian embassy. That I refused to do, and it was only when he was brought into contact with the police through the ordinary course of the police work that they were permitted to listen to his story and take notes from him.

Mr. Speaker, before I
proceed with the speech that I had intended to deliver I should like to ask for your ruling on a point of order, and, of course, to be governed by it. I thought I would be the first speaker on the government side to follow the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and to reply to a motion of want of confidence moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). There has been injected into the debate discussion on a question which was raised on the main motion and nothing whatsoever has been said with regard to the amendment itself. What I should like to know is, am I in order to speak for more than forty minutes? I should like to know that before I begin because I had intended to review some of my experiences in Europe. If I am restricted to forty minutes I shall do it at some other time.

Speaking for this party,
I may say we shall offer no. objection if the Minister of Agriculture requires more than forty minutes to make his reply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think it is
important. It is not a matter of consent. It is a question of the rules of the house and a matter of right. I think the Speaker ought to decide it. I believe the rule is that any member of the government replying to a motion of want of confidence has whatever length of time he wishes to speak if he is the first person to speak after the motion is made.

The Minister of Justice spoke for only a little more than forty minutes, including his answer to the question which was put to him. Therefore I believe that if the Minister of Agriculture wants to answer for the government it is his privilege under standing order 37 to speak for more than forty minutes.

I do not know whether that is your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I have no objection to the minister exceeding his time to-night, because we want to hear about this agricultural policy, but we do not want a ruling which will establish a precedent in this connection. It seems to me the rule is very clear:
. . . such minister, or ia member making a motion of "no confidence" in the government and a minister replying thereto, shall speak for more than forty minutes at a time in any debate.
It seems to me the * minister who speaks immediately after the motion of want of confidence has been moved is the minister replying to the motion.	.

If I may be permitted, the question I raised was in regard to a minister who was not replying at all to the motion of want of confidence. I wanted to know whether in that case I would have the right to speak for more than forty minutes. I should like to have that clear. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I refer you and the house, Mr. Speaker, to a ruling which will be found on pages 22 and 23 of the Journals of the House of Commons, 1941-42, in which the Speaker of the day ruled that as many as six ministers of the crown whose departments were under attack in a want of confidence motion could each reply for more than forty minutes.

May I say one word with respect to this matter. First of all, let it be clear that we want the Minister of Agriculture to have all the time he wishes this evening. With respect to the decision you. sir, are about to give on the technical point raised, I suggest that the Prime Minister spoke after I did the other day, and no doubt spoke for the government in reply to that motion of want of confidence. If there is some rule that six ministers each may speak for more than forty minutes, that is another matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Apart from what my hon. friend says, another motion was moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party.
But was that a motion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly it was a motion in the nature of a want of confidence motion.

The Speaker has been asked for a ruling, and with the permission of the house I shall give that ruling.

The Address-Mr. Gardiner

May I just say this, Mr. Speaker. I was on my feet and sat down because you rose; I did not wish to be disrespectful to the Chair, but I would point out that if mine was a want of confidence motion then I had the right to speak for more than forty minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But you did not do so.

I have been denied that privilege on other occasions in this house; the ruling of Mr. Speaker is there to confirm that statement. Consequently there can be only one want of confidence motion before the house, and I moved an amendment to it. The government cannot have it both ways.

I believe the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is right when he says that a member moving a motion of want of confidence in the government is entitled to speak for more than forty minutes. When the hon. gentleman spoke I did not ask him to resume his seat because he had spoken for more than forty minutes. I was asked by the Minister of Agriculture for a . -'ing as to whether he might speak for more then forty minutes. The question now before the house is the amendment and the subamendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) respectively. The Minister of Justice did not answer for the government in regard to the amendment or the subamendment, so that I believe it is the privilege of the Minister of Agriculture to answer for the government. Therefore he is entitled to speak for more than forty minutes if he wishes to do so.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
Sit down.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I wish to call attention-
If the hon. member will resume his seat, he knows perfectly well that the ruling of the Speaker is not debatable, so that he cannot raise the question now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The ruling is wrong.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
My desire was to have the question cleared up before I began my remarks, in order that I might govern myself accordingly; and I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the ruling you have given.
In discussing the question raised by the amendment and subamendment I desire to deal with the situation referred to in the speech from the throne, which has been commented upon by those who have been discussing this matter and particularly by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). In his remarks dealing with food he made this statement, as reported at page 27 of Hansard of March 18:
I now come to a discussion of agriculture and food. The speech from ithe throne tells us that the most pressing problem demanding immediate attention is the food problem. That is a fact we have known' for months-(that is, everybody except the government. We heard about their new policy first in the speech from the throne.
I do not know whether that remark was intended to leave the impression it left with me, which was that the speech from the throne was referring to a condition which related more particularly to Canada. The speech from the throne had this to say:
Of world problems demanding 'immediate action, the most pressing as the provision of food to those peoples facing acute shortage, and, in some regions, widespread famine. The chance of a peaceful reconstruction of the world depends on food. The shortage at the present time is very great. The problem, moreover, is not only for the next few months, but also for the next few years.
With this statement appearing in the speech from the throne I am in entire agreement, and I wish to 'ay a word in regard to discussions in which I took tsrt during the last session. Last fall, when we We.e discussing in this house whether we should have rationing of meat I made a statement which was quoted in the press from one end of Canada to the other and commented upon by quite a number of newspapers. I repeated a remark I had heard a few days previously made by a minister of the gospel in one of the churches of this city, to the effect that there was a possibility there might be as many as three hundred thousand children 'on the continent of Europe who would lose their lives as a result of starvation, particularly in those areas with which we in this country are concerned, unless something was done to jAovide them with more food than it was then apparent they were going to receive. Since making that remark I have had the privilege of visiting most of the countries I had in mind when making that statement, and I think I am in duty bound to make some report to the house in regard to what I found in that particular area and the effect upon any policies the government may be called upon to announce now in regard to foodstuffs and their distribution.
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

During the six or seven weeks I was on the other side of the ocean I had the privilege of travelling across Great Britain at two different points by car, and of travelling by train throughout the length of the greater part of the island known as Great Britain. I also had the privilege of covering a considerable part of France, of Belgium, of Holland; and of Denmark, as well as a considerable part of Germany both by aeroplane and by automobile.
I did not do as I was warned not to do when I was in, Paris. A guide who was taking me about the city said, "Do not. go back to Canada and say what one other person said who was here in Paris lately, upon returning, to the United States." I asked the guide what had been said, and I was told that particular person had lived at the Ritz hotel.-where I myself was stopping-had gone back to this continent and had made the statement, which had appeared in the press, to the effect that conditions were no worse in Paris than they were on this continent.
With that warning I was careful not to remain all my time in the Ritz hotel. I drove out into the country districts of France and other countries, in so far as it was possible for me to do so, and visited in those country places as well. I took my meals not only in the Ritz hotel, and in other hotels similarly situated, but took some of them in country districts, in ordinary restaurants, just as anyone would walk in off a street and order a meal. On other occasions I was at farm houses when meals were being served. While I did not have meals in all those farm houses, be-cau.se I was not invited in some, yet I did stand and watch people who were eating their meals in houses where 1 was not invited. Therefore I did gain some knowledge as to what conditions are in the areas I visited.
In addition to that, I had an opportunity to visit with men who have been placed in charge of the occupied areas in Germany, and with men who are looking after food supplies in some other sections. What I wish to report to the house is this, that each one of the men I interviewed, who had responsible positions in connection with the distribution of food, and all those with whom I came in contact, assured me that no one had died from starvation in those areas, at least since the armies moved from active battles of warfare to occupation.
I state that merely to impress upon the minds of members of the house and of the people of Canada generally the reports that were made, and the results of what I myself saw. I hope that the decision which we did reach last year, and similar decisions reached
(Mr. Gardiner.]
in other countries did have the effect of placing sufficient food at the disposal of those who are administering those areas, to avoid having children dying from starvation.
But having said that, I would not wish members of the House of Commons to conclude that there is no hardship, that there is no trouble on the continent of Europe in the matter of food supplies. There are very serious difficulties, as the speech from the throne indicates, and I am sure that we as a people have a desire to do everything we possibly can in order to right a condition which does exist there, and to do it as rapidly as possible.
But in order to impress further upon the minds of hon. members what I believe to be the condition there, may I say this, that one can say the worst of which he could conceive with regard to conditions in certain spots or in certain areas, more or less limited so far as their effect upon the population as a whole is concerned. For example, if one is in the centre of the city of Hamburg, where there has been great destruction, he will see smoke-stacks sticking out of basements, with smoke belching from them, indicating that there are people living under the rubble covering the basements of buildings which were blasted by bombing.
No doubt there is great hardship there, and perhaps great difficulty in getting sufficient food to those people. But on the other hand one can go into the rural districts in the different countries about which I have spoken, and sometimes even into the smaller urban communities, sometimes even into sections of cities, and find that the people who are living in those particular areas have sufficient food to ward off anything in the nature of starvation. In some places one even finds it possible to receive meals that are just as good as those received by the American who stopped only in the Ritz hotel, and who went back to America and reported that one can be just as well fed there as he could be anywhere on this continent.
Well, then, you may ask me what the great difficulties are in connection with the situation. I would say they are threefold. First, there has been great damage done to the transportation systems. And even where food is available, in certain areas it is almost impossible to have it transported to other areas where it may be in great need.
In addition to that, there is the difficulty in connection with exchange. Some of the people who are there have been supplied with funds during a time when a government which does not now exist issued currency. As a result of that, there is great difficulty in disposing of

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
commodities for a currency which will be accepted at its face value by those who have it for distribution.
Then there is a most serious condition, one with which we are most concerned here, namely that there is not sufficient food in any event to feed all the people in those areas as they ought to be fed, even when we take into consideration the amount which under present conditions we are able to ship to them.
Those are the three outstanding difficulties, as I see them; and they are the difficulties which must be overcome before people can be properly fed. Indeed, two of them must be overcome before they can be properly fed, even if we supply the full quantity of food required in those districts.
I wish to say something at this time respecting the control conducted by the armies of occupation in those three sections of Germany at which I had the pleasure of looking for a short time, and over limited areas. I was along with officials who gave me whatever information was available in connection with the matter.
I feel that we have in the administration of the three armies of occupation, in so far as I was able to see them working, as complete -and as effective an organization as can be set up for the distribution or ioou unaer rne conditions existing on the continent of Europe.
I say that in order to indicate that possibly we can best meet the situation which exists there by putting any food we have available for distribution in that area-so long as those armies of occupation are in charg.-at the disposal of those who have been p aced there to administer its distribution, rather than by placing it there in some other way.
In addition to that, I shou'd like to say I was agreeably surprised a' the provision made in camps in which p-ople have been congregated by the occupation forces, to take care of people who came, we will say, into Berlin, ahead of the armies. They are being taken care of by those who are in charge of the administration in the certain sections of that city.
I had the privilege of going through one of those camps in which five thousand of those people were congregated, and of seeing conditions there at first hand. I need only say that the property upon which they were congregated is the barracks in which the German army in that section had been trained since possibly the time of Bismarck. The buildings are Veil constructed and the equipment for taking care of 6,000 people is all that one could expect in any refugee camp or any organized camp anywhere. What this reminded 63260-7
me of more than anything else I had ever seen was my experience in Winnipeg when we had people coming to this country from central European countries in hundreds of thousands during a twelve month period. I used to go down to the immigration hall in Winnipeg and see people who had just come off the trains seated about on the floor, on benches, on whatever equipment they may have had, on bundles of clothing or anything else they might have with them. These people were living under exactly the same kind of conditions and they looked like the same type of people. They seemed to be just about as well satisfied as you could have people who are forced away from home.
Another thing that surprised me more than anything else was that the British government, which was the government that had charge of this particular camp, was not only taking care of and clothing all these people, as well as feeding them, but had schools organized with school teachers teaching the children. I must say that the children in those schools showed by the satisfaction on their faces that they were being as well treated and as well cared for as any group of children could be under the conditions that exist when an army has moved across a country and npAnlo I

	, <=u m ahead of the army and
must be taken care of until they "an be redistributed back to where they came tram or somewhere else.

The remainder of it should be framed as the farewell message of His Excellency.
During the six years of war many members on this side of the house refrained from severe criticism of the government. Possibly we erred on the side of leniency, but we did not want to do anything that might possibly interfere with the war effort. Many times suggestions made in good faith were disregarded. During the session of last fall I for one took the stand that on the basis of certain promises the electors of this country, may I say for better or worse, had returned the government to office and therefore the government should be given an opportunity to wind up the business that had been left unfinished at the time of dissolution and to prepare their plans to fulfil their promises. But look at the speech from the throne, as barren as the minds that conceived it.
For my part the truce is over; the gloves are off. I would be unworthy of the trust placed in me by the great majority of the

The Address-Mr. Burton
people I have the honour to represent were I to remain silent any longer. When I think of those who died so that the rest of us could continue to live our way of life; when I think of those who were fortunate enough to return, and when I think of the hard work and the suffering and the sacrifices made by the vast majority of them, I would be neglectful of my duty if I did not protest against the inadequacy of the government's methods of dealing with our many problems, especially in view of the fact that during the past year and more we have been urging the government to prepare for the needs of peace. But the government has been so deaf to our warnings, so determined to follow its own course, which apparently was the line of least resistance, that it now finds itself unprepared to meet the problems which confront us and which have confronted us during the past six months or more. Those problems are becoming worse at an alarming rate. Thousands of our people are drifting back to the conditions which they had to endure during the 1930's.
The capitalist system-
Do not blame the capitalist system. Blame it on the government.

The capitalist system of so-called free enterprise failed the people before the war; it failed the nation during the time of war, and it will inevitably bring disaster to the people and to the nation unless we hasten to replace it before it breaks down completely with a system of social democracy which will give us economic democracy as well as political democracy, a system that will serve the needs of the people and the nation instead of the whims and insatiable desires of the few.
I pause for a moment to refer to something which the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), the leader of the Social Credit party said this afternoon. He is reported in the Evening Citizen to have said, and it is headlined "Social Credit or Communism is His Thesis":
There is no other alternative for the future;
it is social credit or communism.
I am convinced that there is a middle way between those two. He went on to say:
From now on capitalism and free enterprise must compete with communism.
I am also informed that he said that Christian democracy was synonymous with free enterprise, and if I am misquoting him I hope he will correct me. May I point out to him that there are many Christians who believe that private enterprise should not be allowed to dominate and exploit the people.
Hear, hear; I believe that.

I could give him quotations from leaders of many religious denominations along that very line, but I shall give only one with which I am familiar:
It is rightfully contended that certain forms of property must be reserved to the state since they carry with them the opportunity for domination -too great to be left in the hands of private individuals without -injury to the community -at large.
Who said that?

His holiness the late Pope Pius XI in Quadragesimo Anno. I draw attention to that, -Mr. Speaker, because there are so many abuses and terrible things committed under the capitalistic system that those of us who know what is going on cannot as Christians continue to tolerate those conditions and the things -that brought them about. I have always been anxious to give every hon. gentleman a chance to stand for the things in which he believed, but I contend that when we have conditions as grave as we have had for years under the capitalist system, when we have the suffering and the privation and the want that we have had, surely those who are trying to find a better way, a middle way, should not . always be sniped at. I have said that the capitalist system has failed us in the past. Do I need to bring any proof of that? If so, I call on the million or more of those who were on relief in this country in the so-called hungry thirties. I call on those who were in the soup-kitchen lines. I call on those who were dispossessed of their life savings, and on those who were dispossessed of their homes. Do I need to bring any more proof? Then I would remind the house of the 42 per cent of our young men who in the early days of the war were rejected for military service because of physical disabilities most of which \yere brought on by malnutrition during those depression years.
